message:
QUESTION:
Did guard X's three-point shooting genuinely improve after the mid-season change of shooting coach, and should X take a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season?

DATA:
Professional basketball. Guard X's shooting before and after a mid-season change of shooting coach, which took effect after game 30. X played in all 50 games. His minutes per game were similar in both periods (about 32).

Shooting percentage = makes / attempts.

| | Games 1-30 | Games 31-50 |
| Three-point attempts | 150 | 80 |
| Three-point makes | 51 | 32 |
| Free-throw attempts | 100 | 70 |
| Free-throw makes | 80 | 55 |

League average three-point percentage this season: 36%.

Opponent breakdown: in games 31-50, 30 of X's 80 three-point attempts came in 4 games against the league's two worst-ranked perimeter defences, and he made 18 of those 30. X did not face either of those teams in games 1-30.

The coaching staff must decide whether to increase X's share of team three-point attempts next season. The new shooting coach worked with the whole squad, not just X.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] A 6-point rise from 34% is 6/34 = 17.6% in relative terms, not 21%. CORRECTION: Relative improvement of about 18%.
F2. [omission] Ignores that 30 of the 80 post-change attempts (18 made) came against the two worst perimeter defences, which X did not face before the change. CORRECTION: Against other opponents after the change X made 14 of 50 (28%), below his pre-change 34%. The apparent improvement is driven by schedule.
F3. [misreport] The data show free throws went from 80/100 = 80% to 55/70 = 78.6%, a slight fall. CORRECTION: Free-throw shooting did not improve, so it provides no corroboration of better mechanics.
F4. [inference] Draws a causal, stable conclusion from 80 attempts. The pre/post difference is not statistically significant (two-proportion z of about 0.9), it is confounded by opponent quality, and the coach changed for the whole squad. CORRECTION: The evidence is consistent with no change in X's true shooting ability. No reallocation of attempts is justified on these data.

EXTENSIONS:
- Give interval estimates: 32/80 has a 95% CI of roughly 29-51%, and 51/150 of roughly 26-42%. The intervals overlap heavily, which shows how little 20 games can establish.
- Use the whole squad as a comparison. Since the coach worked with everyone, compare teammates' pre/post three-point percentages (ideally against the same opponents) to separate a coaching effect from schedule effects.
- Apply regression to the league mean (e.g. empirical-Bayes shrinkage towards 36% based on attempts) to estimate X's likely true rate before setting next season's shot allocation.

FINAL VERSION:
# Guard X: Three-Point Shooting Since the Coaching Change

**Summary.** The data do not show that X's three-point shooting genuinely improved after the coaching change. His rise from 34% to 40% comes entirely from four games against the league's two weakest perimeter defences. Against all other opponents he shot 28% on 50 attempts, no better than before the change. His free-throw percentage dipped slightly. Over the full season he shot 36.1%, but without the four weak-defence games he shot 32.5%. The fairest description is a shooter who is at best league average and possibly a little below. The evidence does not support giving him a larger share of the team's threes next season.

**Before and after: headline figures**

| | Games 1-30 | Games 31-50 | Season |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3PT makes / attempts | 51 / 150 | 32 / 80 | 83 / 230 |
| 3PT % | 34.0% | 40.0% | 36.1% |
| 3PT attempts per game | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.6 |
| FT makes / attempts | 80 / 100 | 55 / 70 | 135 / 170 |
| FT % | 80.0% | 78.6% | 79.4% |

His three-point percentage rose by 6 points, a relative rise of about 18%. He played all 50 games at about 32 minutes per game, so availability and playing time do not explain the change.

**Opponent mix explains the rise.** In games 31-50, 30 of X's 80 attempts came in four games against the league's two worst perimeter defences. He did not face either team in games 1-30.

| Games 31-50 | Makes / attempts | 3PT % | Attempts per game |
|---|---|---|---|
| vs two worst perimeter defences (4 games) | 18 / 30 | 60.0% | 7.5 |
| vs all other opponents (16 games) | 14 / 50 | 28.0% | 3.1 |
| **All games 31-50** | **32 / 80** | **40.0%** | **4.0** |

So the two periods are not like for like.

- **Against other opponents in games 31-50 he shot 28%.** That is no better than his pre-change 34%. It is also below the league's 36%, but that gap is within normal variation (z ≈ 1.2).
- **The weak-defence games carry the whole apparent gain.** He took far more threes in those games (7.5 per game against 3.1), which suggests those opponents gave him open looks. Even so, 60% is well above what even poor perimeter defences usually allow, and 30 attempts is a small sample. Luck very likely played a part as well. The post-change rise therefore rests on a sample that was both easy and noisy.
- **Caveat on the baseline.** The comparison assumes the opponents in games 1-30 were broadly similar to the 16 "other" opponents later. We know only that the two weakest defences were absent from games 1-30. That period could still have had an unusually strong or weak schedule in other ways.

**Sample size.** Even at face value, the move from 34% to 40% is within normal variation. The standard error of the difference is about 6.7 points, so z ≈ 0.9 and p ≈ 0.37. The drop from 34% to 28% against other opponents is not significant either (SE ≈ 7.4 points, z ≈ 0.8). So the apparent improvement disappears once the schedule is accounted for, but the data do not show that X got worse.

**Free throws show no improvement.** His free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% to 78.6%, a change well within noise. Free throws are a defence-free check on shooting mechanics, and they show no sign of a mechanical gain. They would not capture three-point-specific coaching, such as footwork off screens, release speed or shot selection. So they are neutral evidence, not evidence against improvement.

**What is X's true level?** The full-season 36.1% includes the same weak-defence games that inflate the post-change figure. Those four games are 8% of his games but 13% of his attempts, because he shot far more often against those teams. Without them he shot 65/200 = 32.5%. Every team plays some weak defences, so the full-season number isn't simply wrong. It is the generous end of a range. The 32.5% figure is itself within noise of the league average (z ≈ 1.0). A fair reading is that X is roughly a 32.5–36% shooter: at best league average, possibly a little below.

**Expected value.** At 36.1%, an X three is worth about 1.08 points per attempt, which is league average. At 32.5% it is worth about 0.98. His realistic value is therefore roughly 0.98–1.08 points per attempt. The post-change 40% would imply 1.20 points per attempt, but that rate was inflated by the schedule and a small sample, so it should not drive decisions.

**The question about share of attempts.** X's share of the team's threes depends on how he compares with his teammates, and these data do not cover that.

- **The new coach worked with the whole squad.** If teammates also improved, X's relative standing may not have changed. We need teammates' before-and-after rates, adjusted for opponents in the same way.
- **Moving attempts to X helps only if his threes are better than the shots they replace.** On current evidence he is at best a league-average shooter. Whether that beats the alternatives depends on teammates' rates, which we don't have.

**Other limitations.**

- **No shot-level data.** These are season totals only. They say nothing about shot difficulty (catch-and-shoot versus off the dribble, contested versus open) or shot location.
- **Falling volume.** Against ordinary opponents his attempts fell from 5.0 to 3.1 per game. That could reflect a role or lineup change after game 30. It could also mean the new coach steered him away from low-quality attempts. Better shot selection can add real value even when shooting percentage stays flat, so this deserves a look before judging the coach's effect on X.

**Recommendation.**

1. **Do not increase X's share of three-point attempts on the basis of these data.** The apparent improvement comes entirely from four games against weak defences. Without them, his post-change shooting is no better than before.
2. **Plan around X as a roughly 32.5–36% three-point shooter, at best league average,** until better evidence arrives.
3. **Before revisiting the decision, gather:**
   - opponent-adjusted three-point rates for X and his teammates, before and after the coaching change;
   - shot-quality and shot-selection data (defender distance, catch-and-shoot share, shot location, attempt mix), to separate better shooting from easier or better-chosen shots;
   - a larger sample: review X's opponent-adjusted rate after 20-30 games next season, and keep tracking his free-throw percentage as a defence-free check.
4. **Keep him working with the new shooting coach.** Nothing here suggests harm, and the coach's value is better judged across the whole squad than from one player's split.
